President Trump on Friday defended the Justice Department's $1.7 billion "anti-weaponization" fund and said he "gave up a lot of money" by allowing its creation. description_long: On May 22, 2026, Trump defended the Justice Department’s $1.7 billion Anti-Weaponization Fund and said he had allowed it to proceed, after twice saying earlier that week that he was not involved in its creation or negotiation. He said he could have received a large settlement in his suit over the IRS leak of his tax returns but chose to help others instead. The White House distinguished his claimed role in allowing a settlement from involvement in designing the fund. DOJ said the fund would hear claims of weaponization, with payments decided by a board appointed by the attorney general; it had not yet supplied full operating and eligibility details. Senate Republicans pressed Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche for information, and some senators raised concern that pardoned January 6 defendants convicted of assaulting officers could receive payments. The record documents Trump’s public defense and the change in how he described his role, not an audited calculation of the money he said he gave up or a settled account of who would qualify.
notes: CBS News reports Trump earlier denied involvement in the fund's creation and later said he allowed it to proceed. It quotes the White House distinguishing those claims and reports that eligibility and operation details remained unsettled; the amount Trump said he gave up is not independently calculated.

title: A Chaotic Cabinet: Four Major Departures in Six Months
description_short: A Chaotic Cabinet: Four Major Departures in Six Months
description_medium: By late June 2026, the instability of Trump's second-term Cabinet became glaringly obvious. Within just the first half of the year, four top officials had either been fired or resigned under pressure: Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem (fired), Attorney General Pam Bondi (removed), Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer (resigned amidst an IG probe), and DNI Tulsi Gabbard (resigned over Iran). This unprecedented turnover left critical departments rudderless and run by unconfirmed acting secretaries like Todd Blanche at the DOJ, allowing Trump to bypass Senate confirmation and consolidate executive power.
